title: A fair ticket sale
brief: Design a ticket booking service for a global concert launch. Users search events, reserve seats briefly and pay without overselling.
context: A stadium has 60,000 seats; 2 million buyers may arrive in the first minute.
Payment confirmation can arrive after a reservation expires. Customers refresh aggressively.
The business values fair access and correct inventory over a perfectly fresh seat map.
followUps: The payment provider times out after charging the buyer. How do you reconcile this without issuing two tickets?
A hot event overwhelms one inventory partition. What protects the authoritative write path?
The primary region fails during checkout. Which operations remain available?
debrief: Separate cached discovery from authoritative inventory. An atomic conditional transition can reserve an available seat with an expiry and version.
Treat payment and booking as a recoverable workflow: idempotency keys, durable events, reconciliation and explicit refund rules for late payments.
A waiting room and admission control protect capacity. Quantify the hot key limit; partitioning alone does not solve contention on a single seat.
Alert on reservation-to-payment latency, oversell invariants, queue age and reconciliation backlog; enforce per-user limits and audit access.

title: Reliable notifications
brief: Design a multi-channel notification platform for transactional email, SMS and push with user preferences.
context: 10 million users receive an average of 8 messages daily; product launches create 20× peaks.
Password reset messages should arrive within seconds. Marketing messages can wait.
Providers may duplicate callbacks, throttle requests or fail for an hour.
followUps: A provider accepts a message but the request times out. Can you promise exactly-once delivery?
A user opts out while a campaign is queued. Where is consent checked?
One tenant sends 90% of traffic. How do you preserve other tenants’ latency?
debrief: Separate priority queues and per-tenant quotas; estimate throughput and peak drain time rather than provisioning from daily averages.
Persist message intent and idempotency identifiers. At-least-once processing plus deduplication reduces duplicates but cannot guarantee external exactly-once delivery.
Check consent at send time, minimize retained content and protect reset links; give retries a bounded lifetime.
Measure end-to-end age by priority, delivery success, suppression and provider error rates; include dead-letter inspection and replay controls.

title: Team file sharing
brief: Design a secure team file sharing service with large uploads, version history and expiring share links.
context: Five million users store an average of 2 GB each. Files range from 1 KB to 10 GB.
A team can revoke a public link immediately; some users work on unreliable networks.
Customers request audit history and a defined deletion policy.
followUps: An upload completes but the metadata transaction fails. How are orphaned objects cleaned up?
A revoked link still has a cached download response. What guarantee can you make?
Two people edit the same version offline. How does your product surface the conflict?
debrief: Keep binary objects in object storage and metadata, versions and access rules in an indexed transactional store. Use resumable multipart upload with checksums.
Make upload completion idempotent and reconcile orphaned parts; distinguish garbage collection from user-visible deletion and retention obligations.
Use short-lived scoped download credentials and authorize each link resolution. CDN lifetime bounds revocation guarantees; document that tradeoff.
Use optimistic concurrency for conflicting versions; audit security-sensitive events without logging secrets and monitor failed uploads, authorization denials and storage growth.

title: Near-real-time metrics
brief: Design a product analytics pipeline that ingests events and serves near-real-time dashboards.
context: 100,000 events per second at peak, about 500 bytes each. Keep raw events for 30 days.
Dashboards show minute-level aggregates by tenant; a few tenants dominate volume.
Events arrive late, out of order and sometimes duplicated.
followUps: A client changes its clock and sends events dated tomorrow. How are windows handled?
A dashboard total differs after a backfill. How do you explain and verify the correction?
A tenant asks to delete one person’s historical events. Where is identity retained?
debrief: Estimate peak ingest at 50 MB/s and distinguish peak from sustained storage assumptions. Separate durable ingestion, stream processing and query-serving aggregates.
Use event identifiers, event and receive times, a lateness policy and versioned schemas; state whether results are provisional.
Partition to handle hot tenants; use bounded cardinality and preaggregation instead of promising arbitrary low-latency queries.
Plan backfill isolation, reconciliation, deletion propagation, tenant access control and freshness/lag alerts with traceable pipeline lineage.

title: Reduce onboarding drop-off
brief: A bank wants an “AI onboarding assistant” because only 45% of started applications reach completion. Discover the actual problem and propose an MVP.
context: Compliance requires identity checks before activation. Operations reports many manual reviews.
Sales wants fewer questions; risk wants more evidence. The sponsor wants launch in six weeks.
The available funnel data does not distinguish voluntary exits from technical failures.
followUps: Compliance says a proposed shortcut breaches policy. How do you make the tradeoff visible?
The sponsor calls all features “must-have.” Show a defensible MVP cut.
Completion rises after launch, but a marketing campaign changed the applicant mix. How do you evaluate value?
debrief: Establish funnel definitions, customer segments and exit reasons before accepting the AI solution. Interview applicants, risk, support and operations.
Map handoffs and exception queues. Write acceptance criteria for missing documents, failed verification and accessible recovery.
Prioritize verified sources of friction with risk gates, effort and dependencies. Keep required controls and record the decision owner.
Trace UAT to requirements with synthetic identity data. Compare cohorts or an experiment, while tracking review effort, fraud and completion as guardrails.

title: Fix a returns process
brief: An online retailer receives complaints about slow refunds. Warehouse and finance teams blame one another. Lead analysis of the returns process.
context: Customers see “received” before warehouse inspection is complete. Finance batches refunds nightly.
Exceptions are handled in spreadsheets; some returns have no order reference.
A new system must be delivered before the holiday peak.
followUps: Warehouse wants mandatory inspection for every item; finance wants automatic refunds. How do you resolve this?
An order contains two items but only one was returned. Write a UAT example.
The average refund time improves while the longest waits worsen. What do you report?
debrief: Map event definitions, queue waits, handoffs and exception ownership from return initiation to settled refund. Validate complaints with segment-level data.
Separate customer status from internal processing state. Acceptance criteria should cover partial returns, duplicate scans, missing references and failed refunds.
Compare risk-based automation against universal inspection; prioritize a traceable happy path plus owned exception handling before peak.
UAT should reconcile item, amount and payment records. Measure median and tail refund times, rework, errors and contact rate against a baseline.

title: Clinic scheduling modernization
brief: A clinic network wants to replace telephone appointment booking with a self-service portal. Define a safe, valuable first release.
context: Reception staff handle cancellations and urgent requests differently across clinics.
Some patients need interpreters or cannot use a smartphone. Specialist appointments need referrals.
The sponsor wants lower call volume without increasing missed or inappropriate appointments.
followUps: A clinic insists its exception is unique. How do you test whether customization is necessary?
Two patients select the final slot simultaneously. Specify expected behavior.
Call volume falls but no-shows rise. How should success be judged?
debrief: Elicit needs from patients, reception, clinicians and scheduling administrators; capture accessibility and assisted-channel needs.
Model slot availability, referral rules, cancellations and urgent triage. Define observable conflict handling and role permissions.
Choose a constrained appointment type or pilot clinic based on value and risk; document out-of-scope flows and dependencies on the record system.
Use synthetic patient records in UAT, test double booking and referral failures, and assign clinical sign-off. Measure call effort with access, no-show and safety guardrails.

title: One trusted revenue report
brief: Finance and sales publish conflicting monthly revenue figures. The CFO asks for a single dashboard. Establish requirements and a delivery plan.
context: Sales counts signed contracts; finance recognizes revenue over the service period.
Currencies, credits and late adjustments are handled inconsistently.
Executives want the dashboard in four weeks and insist existing reports are correct.
followUps: The CFO asks you to remove reconciliation to meet the date. What options do you present?
A credit note arrives after month close. Specify how historical totals should behave.
How can a dashboard’s business value be measured beyond page views?
debrief: Treat conflicting definitions as a business rule problem. Agree measures, grain, cutoff, currency and authoritative data owners before designing visuals.
Map lineage and adjustment controls. Specify recognized revenue separately from bookings and label the period and refresh status.
Prioritize reconciled core figures, documented exceptions and access control; make confidence and unresolved variances visible.
UAT should reconcile signed-off samples including FX, credits and late changes. Measure reporting effort, decision turnaround and variance resolution with accountable owners.

title: Ownership beyond your remit
brief: Tell me about a time you took ownership of a problem that crossed team boundaries.
context: Use a real work, volunteering or study example. Do not invent scale or responsibility.
Explain why intervention mattered and how you avoided bypassing the accountable owner.
followUps: What did you personally do that would not otherwise have happened?
Who disagreed with your approach and how did you involve them?
What remained unresolved, and how did you hand over ownership?
debrief: A strong story states the gap, stakes and your bounded responsibility before describing the intervention.
Explain alignment and escalation, not only heroic extra hours. Distinguish your actions from others’ work.
Use an honest outcome and describe a durable owner, process or monitoring change; reflect on whether earlier alignment would have helped.

title: Disagree and commit
brief: Tell me about a meaningful disagreement with a colleague or stakeholder and how you handled it.
context: Choose a disagreement with real stakes, not a harmless preference.
Represent the other person’s reasoning fairly and protect confidential details.
followUps: What evidence would have changed your mind?
What did you do after the decision went against your preferred option?
How did the relationship change, and what feedback did you receive?
debrief: Explain the competing goals and your assumptions without making the other person a villain.
Describe listening, evidence and a decision mechanism. Escalation may be appropriate when ownership or risk requires it.
A credible conclusion can be a compromise or a decision you opposed. Show professional follow-through and a specific lesson about working together.

title: A failure you owned
brief: Tell me about a mistake or failed initiative for which you were personally accountable.
context: Choose an example where your decision or omission mattered.
Focus on accountability, repair and changed behavior; avoid confidential incident details.
followUps: When did you first know the approach was failing and whom did you tell?
Which consequence was not repaired?
Give a later example that demonstrates you changed your behavior.
debrief: State the intended result, your decision and what actually happened without shifting responsibility.
Explain containment, communication and repair proportionately; acknowledge harm that remained.
Connect root cause to a concrete habit or system change. A later example is stronger evidence of learning than saying you now “communicate more.”

title: Returning to work
brief: Rehearse how you would describe your return to work after a career break, and an example showing readiness for the role.
context: Share only the personal context you choose. A brief neutral description of the break is sufficient.
You may use recent study, volunteering, caregiving logistics or earlier work as evidence; label the context honestly.
Focus on transferable skills and current preparation without apologizing for the break.
followUps: Which part of this role would require the most ramp-up, and what is your plan?
Tell me about a recent challenge that demonstrates a relevant skill.
What support or working arrangement helps you do your best work? Share only what you want to disclose.
debrief: Keep the transition explanation concise, voluntary and forward-looking. Personal medical or family details are not required.
Use a specific STAR example with your actions and credible results; do not equate course completion with professional experience.
Explain role-relevant refresh work, an achievable ramp-up plan and the evidence you can discuss. Treat readiness as current skills and learning, not the absence of a career break.
